Acts 2:3 The hate expressed in the murders of three people at the Islamic Cultural Center of San Diego this past Monday, May 18, is antithetical to the spirit of Pentecost, a spirit which celebrates the spiritual value of every human being. In contrast, the response of the members of the Islamic Cultural Center is the epitome of the Spirit of Pentecost. While not Christian, their words are Christ like, speaking of love, care, resilience and hope. In a tribute to her father, Amin Abdullah, the security guard at the center who was killed while trying to protect others, Hawaa Abdullah, spoke of his openness and kindness to all people. “Muslim, Christian, Jewish, those with no faith, he didn’t care, he would treat you human to human. He would smile at people he did not know. You can see his happiness, and just who he is a person, just looking at his face.” Iman Taha Hassane said, “This is not going to stop us from showing up, it’s not going to stop us from getting involved and engaged civically and politically and it’s not going to stop us from building bridges with other faith communities.” We need to claim their words as Pentecost words for the spirit of Pentecost is not about religion, ethnicity, creed, culture or class. It is about the divine touch found in simple humanity; the breath of heaven expressed in caring human words. It is about building bridges. It is not about how we worship, it is about how we express our love, where we find our hope. The prophet Joel found hope in the promise of the Spirit that would fall on all flesh. The writer of Acts found hope in the Spirit that would help people from very different backgrounds truly hear each other. John, the prophet of Revelation found hope in the promise that it was the Spirit’s ultimate work to wipe every tear from our eyes. These prophets believed that each of us, regardless of religion or race are trusted by the Holy One to sense the Spirit, see the Spirit and share the Spirit, not just at Pentecost but on all days, especially those days when hate is on the march, when hurt is abundant and hope seems far away. articles.text: Done are the toils and the wearisome marches, Done is the summons of bugle and drum. Softly and sweetly the sky overarches, Shelt’ring a land where Rebellion is dumb. Dark were the days of the country’s derangement, Sad were the hours when the conflict was on, But through the gloom of fraternal estrangement God sent his light, and we welcome the dawn. O’er the expanse of our mighty dominions, Sweeping away to the uttermost parts, Peace, the wide-flying, on untiring pinions, Bringeth her message of joy to our hearts. Ah, but this joy which our minds cannot measure, What did it cost for our fathers to gain! Bought at the price of the heart’s dearest treasure, Born out of travail and sorrow and pain; Born in the battle where fleet Death was flying, Slaying with sabre-stroke bloody and fell; Born where the heroes and martyrs were dying, Torn by the fury of bullet and shell. Ah, but the day is past; silent the rattle, And the confusion that followed the fight. Peace to the heroes who died in the battle, Martyrs to truth and the crowning of Right! Out of the blood of a conflict fraternal, Out of the dust and dimness of death, Burst into blossoms of glory eternal Flowers that sweeten the world with the breath. Flowers of charity, peace, and devotion Bloom in the hearts that are empty of strife; Love that is boundless and broad as the ocean Leaps into beauty and fullness of life. So, with the singing of paeans and chorals, And with the flag flashing high in the sun, Place on the graves of our heroes the laurels Which their unfaltering valor has won!

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has released its proposed budget for the FY2026-2027. The City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee met this week to review the proposed budget. The Committee will provide the City Council with its findings and recommendations in advance of budget adoption. The City Council will discuss the proposed budget at two public hearings in June: Monday, June 1, 6 p.m., and Monday, June 15, 6 p.m. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. Finance Director Kiran Bawa will present this year’s budget, her first since being appointed last year. The proposed FY2026-27 budget reflects a transition from major project delivery to longterm stewardship. Over the past several years, the City has advanced a large portfolio of housing policy work and completed an unprecedented number of capital improvements, including two of the largest, most complex projects in Piedmont’s history: the all-electric new Community Pool and the new police and fire Dispatch Center. A key priority for the proposed budget will be securing a development partner for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Transitioning new facilities to sustainable long-term operations by a focus on staffing, service models, managing costs, refining systems based on real-world use, and ensuring these major investments deliver their full potential to the community. The proposed budget features a General Fund of $41.2 million, a 1.3% increase on the current budget. Expenditures are expected to increase by 3% over the current budget. After a transfer of $1 million to the Facilities Maintenance Fund for deferred maintenance and sidewalk repairs in the coming year and $750,000 to the Capital Improvements Fund, the General Fund will experience a Net Loss estimated at $1.0 million. The Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorsing the proposed budget states, “The proposed FY 2026-27 budget reflects another year of meaningful progress toward the City’s long-term strategic priorities, while also recognizing the financial pressures and uncertainties that continue to shape the municipal landscape. Over the past year, the City has advanced several significant capital and operational initiatives that strengthen public infrastructure, improve service delivery, and support community needs.” Looking forward, the Committee is concerned about the current state of the real estate market. Persistent inf lation and elevated interest rates have weakened the housing market and may continue to affect property-related revenues. Approximately 64% of the City’s revenues are tied to property-based taxes. These trends represent a significant fiscal concern. The Committee is concerned that the statewide initiative titled the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act” would present a challenge for Piedmont. The act recently qualified for placement on the November 2026 ballot, and if it passes, it would invalidate all existing municipal real property transfer taxes in charter cities starting December 31, 2028. Loss of this revenue source, which represents roughly 10% of General Fund revenues, would have a profound impact on Piedmont. The City Council will discuss the proposed budget at two public hearings in June. Community members are welcome to attend and speak at the meetings. The City Council is anticipated to adopt the FY2026-27 budget on June 15. Readers can find more details on the budget at the following link: https://piedmont. ca.gov/news/proposed_f_y26- 27_city _budget_ published_ may_2026.

articles.text: Bamboo is a world-class cuddle bug, happily soaking up attention and settling in beside you for a cozy evening at home. This affectionate 14-year-old senior can make leaning against your leg feel like a full-time profession, and at night, happily climbs into bed, curls up beside you, and often rests a paw gently against you just to stay connected. This mellow gentleman would do best in a calm home with someone willing to make a few thoughtful accommodations for his comfort, like low-entry litter boxes and easy-to-access resting spots. Like many seniors, Bamboo has arthritis and kidney disease, and takes daily medication mixed easily into his wet food. Bamboo may be a lovebug, but he also enjoys playtime, such as “enthusiastically batting after wand toys from a comfortable position,” and vibing out to his catnip banana. In return for 5 minutes of toy Adopt Bamboo through Cat Town. time and extended cuddle sessions, he offers gratitude, gentleness, and yes, more cuddles. If he’s feeling overlooked, Bamboo isn’t shy about asking for attention — purring happily once he feels seen and reassured — and he may also enjoy the friendship of another calm cat companion. Bamboo is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org

articles.text: For Julia Banuelos, now a junior at Dartmouth College where she is majoring in psychology and economics, her leadership journey began with the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC). She credits that experience, along with National Youth Leadership Training, with shaping the leader she is today, including her recent election as sorority president. Banuelos joined PCSC as a freshman at Piedmont High School and quickly discovered it was more than a service club. “It was service with friends,” she says. That combination created a unique environment—one that encouraged participation and community service while providing many opportunities to develop leadership skills. Her defining moment came when she became president. Advisor Ken Li asked her one day, What’s your vision? What are your goals? “He helped break down something that felt daunting,” Banuelos said. “You need clarity to lead.” Banuelos is quick to emphasize that PCSC’s success is deeply tied to Li’s mentorship. Known for his dedication to student growth, Li invests hours guiding students through goal setting, decision making, and personal development. He encourages members to stretch beyond their comfort zones—whether that means leading a fundraiser, reaching out to community sponsors, or participating in programs like National Youth Leadership Training. “He truly cares about helping you become the best version of yourself,” Banuelos said. “He’s not just focused on the projects – he’s focused on the people.” PCSC’s student-led structure gave Banuelos meaningful responsibility and opportunities to learn to lead projects, and later as vice president of fundraising and then co-president. She credits coordinating a major service project involving 50-70 volunteers as really building her leadership muscle, especially when it came Julia Banuelos’ first PCSC event volunteering at Bambino Thrift Store which benefits Children’s Hospital, where she learned more about what the Crew was all about in 2019. to organizing, delegating, and managing teams. Banuelos is a big fan of PCSC. “The more you put in, the more you get out, as most things in life. PCSC is self-directed, so you can make it what you want. If you are interested in animal shelters, you can host an event and invite your friends. If you want to do build on that, you can become Julia Banuelos during a High Adventure Crew overnight trip in 2022 VP of Program and create events for the entire Crew. There are so many ways to get involved and help in the community.” Through National Youth Leadership Training, another Scouting program, Banuelos further developed her leadership abilities, progressing from participant to program leader over three summers. The experience pushed her outside her comfort zone and deepened her confidence as a leader. Banuelos said those lessons are also helping her navigate countless opportunities to get involved at Dartmouth. “I know what it feels like to be passionate about something, and I won’t settle for less,” she said. articles.text: Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE), a volunteer-run community of parents dedicated to supporting students with disabilities, has awarded $7,530 in grants to educators across the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD), funding critical tools, resources, and programs that promote inclusive learning environments. Through its annual grants program, PIE invites special education staff from across the district—from preschool through high school and adult transition—to apply for funding to meet the evolving needs of their students. Nearly 100% of funds raised by PIE go directly toward these teacher-driven grants, ensuring meaningful, immediate impact in classrooms. This year’s grants, awarded in partnership with Jean Fagin, Director of Special Education, funded a wide range of initiatives, including: • Specialized Literacy & Curriculum: Orton-Gillingham materials, decodable books, and adapted materials for Earth Sciences, Civics and Economics classes • Staff Resources & Technology: Subscriptions to The Informed SLP and Padlet, giving specialists access to the latest evidence-based tools • Sensory & Emotional Regulation: tactile tools, weighted supports, trampolines, and balance equipment • Community Integration & PIE Board President Betty Rojas (left), PUSD Special Education Director Jean Fagin, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, and PIE Board Vice President and Grants Chair Meredith Lamont Life Skills: off-campus experiences and transition program supplies • Creative Expression & Inclusive Play: toys, games, and art materials to foster engagement and inclusion “These grants are a direct reflection of our community’s generosity,” said Meredith Lamont, Vice President of PIE and Chair of the Grants Committee. “Our donors trust us to put their contributions to work where they matter most. By funding the specific, on-the-ground needs identified by our district’s dedicated special education staff, we’re helping ensure that students with disabilities have the support and resources they need to truly thrive.” PIE (formerly known as PRAISE) partners with families, educators, and PUSD to ensure that students with disabilities and neurodivergences, including those with IEPs and 504 plans, receive the support and resources they need to thrive and belong. Their vision is a Piedmont community where every student feels a deep sense of belonging, inclusion, and support — academically, socially, and emotionally — and where differences are understood, respected, and celebrated. For more information about PIE or to support future grants, visit: Piedmontie.org

Sarah bravely fought breast cancer with Trason constantly by her side. They were married on August 26, 1990, at the Cameron Stanford House at Lake Merritt. The Hawaiian style wedding is fondly remembered by those in attendance. Sarah grew up in Piedmont attended Wildwood Elementary School and graduated in 1985 from Piedmont High School. As a teenager in the 80s, she loved the band Journey and the lead singer Steve Perry. Her happiness was dancing to Journey when they performed at the Oakland Coliseum Day on the Green concerts. In her early twenties Sarah met Trason as they both worked at Sequoyah Country Club. Later she found such joy as an employee at Ladyfingers Bakery. She became a truly gifted baker. Lucky for us, every holiday and birthday was a celebration with her delicious cookies and cakes. For the last 20 years Sarah became a fixture at Piedmont Grocery. Many a friend and loved one insisted on Sarah’s check out register as it often included a warm hug. She was a familiar face to many and loved by all. Sarah also loved to garden and grow her own produce. She found such happiness when cooking from her own garden. Sarah Basconis, a familiar face at Piedmont Grocery for 20 years, died of cancer on April 21, 2026. We often remark that Sarah “grew up with five parents.” Sarah was born when her three siblings were teenagers. As a toddler she was often hoisted onto one of our shoulders for a walk in Piedmont Park. She was the light of our lives and enriched our hearts with her adorable heart. We are forever grateful to witness the life of this amazing woman. Sarah leaves behind her husband Trason Basconis, her brothers Steve Mikkelson and Kris Mikkelson, sister Tracy Mikkelson, sister-in-law Clara Mikkelson and cousin Pamela Perry. She has joined our parents, Milton and Monica Mikkelson in rest. She is greatly loved and will be forever missed. Please visit this website and enjoy and share in her memory. articles.text: Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht reached the NCS Meet of Champions finals in the 200 meter dash. Piedmont High’s track and field team concluded its season at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on Friday and Saturday, May 22-23 at Dublin High. The Highlanders had 11 athletes featured, with runners Claire Aubrecht and Sebastien Swain reaching the finals of their events. In the 200 meter dash, Aubrecht fifth of seven overall with a time of 25.46, coming two spots shy of qualifying for the CIF State meet. To reach the finals, she placed eighth of 23 runners in the preliminary round, clocking a time of 25.55 seconds. “I had the big goal of going to State. This was the first time I made the finals, I’m really happy about that. I missed out on State by two places. Hopefully next year I’ll go. I really wanted to get sixth to be on the podium. I was in Lane 8, so I can’t really see people in my peripheral, but I was close enough to know whether I needed to push a little bit more. I tried to get up to a fast pace at the start, and over on the corner you just float and hold the pace, but then you push out to the corner and use the curve to your advantage—we call it slingshotting,” Aubrecht said. She also placed 10th of 23 runners in the 100 meters in 12.39, further lowering her school-record time. “Getting the school records were my goals for a while, and I really didn’t think I could get it. This year, I was focused on dropping time and the results came. I’m hoping to get to the 12.2s or 12.1s, but I’ll be happy however far I go,” Aubrecht said. Swain’s 800-meter final appearance came with a bit of adversity. After getting boxed in multiple times, he placed eighth of 10 runners in 2:01.53. He was second of 29 runners in the preliminary race with a fast time of 1:55.45—just .12 of a second behind Analy’s Owen Dawson, who won. “I was trying to win this thing,” Swain said after the finals. “The race didn’t go how I wanted, I had a bad start and there was a lot of fighting out there and boxing in and out. That made things a bit difficult, but I understand why it happened. The 2026 season took a lot of perseverance by Swain who was recovering from knee surgery he underwent last summer and rebuilding his endurance from then on. “This was the first back-toback races I’ve done since my surgery. I thought I ran pretty well yesterday, but maybe my fitness isn’t exactly where I want it to be. But I’m still doing alright. This year was a change of mentality for me and how I approach the sport. I had a great season last year, but my injury prevented me from doing endurance work. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end in the first round of the Division 4 NCS playoffs against Livermore. Piedmont High’s baseball season came to an end on Wednesday, May 20. Seeded #6 it lost 4-2 to No. 11 Livermore at Humphries Diamond in the first round of the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs. It was a close game with both teams tied 2-2 going into the final inning, but the Cowboys tacked on their two winning runs in the top of the seventh. It was that kind of season for the Highlanders, having 14 games separated by three runs or less. Piedmont won just four of those games and tied another two. “We’ve gotten down so many times in the first inning and have found a way to claw back. We try to make it a seven-inning game, and it just went their way in the last inning. We’ve been right on that precipice of winning or losing, and it broke the wrong way more times than the right way. With freshmen and sophomores and just a couple of seniors, hopefully it breaks the right way in the future,” coach Eric Olson said. Wednesday’s loss resulted in Piedmont’s fifth defeat in a row. “It was the season in a nutshell. We got into an early deficit and fought back. Just a couple more timely hits would have been huge,” senior Diego Delventhal said. “We’ve had a lot of close games that just didn’t go our way, but the fight is fun. It’s all a part of the game,” senior Jack Meyjes mentioned. Despite the loss, it was a strong game from sophomore pitcher Massimo Mittone, throwing all seven innings. “I tried to battle to the end, it sucks to end the season this way for our seniors. I felt great out there, but there’s a few pitches I wish I had back. The first and last inning didn’t go the greatest, my changeup felt great, but my fastball wasn’t up to par,” Mittone said. Diego Delventhal went 1-for-3 with a stolen base in his final game with Piedmont High. Jack Meyjes went 1-for-2 with one RBI and one run scored in his final Piedmont appearance.

articles.text: Piedmont High named Lucas Smolko and Dahlia Osman as the school’s 2026 Outstanding Senior Athletes recipients, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Tennis player Lucas Smolko won the school’s first boys’ North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since 1975 and became the first Western Alameda County Conference singles champion in three successive years. He was our honorable mention for 2024 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Freshman of the Year. Smolko beat Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen 6-4, 6-3 for the Division 2 NCS singles title. To reach the final, Smolko won 6-0, 6-0 over St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson in the opening round, followed up with a 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and dominated Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His appearance in the NCS title match marked the third of his career. He lost as a freshman to eventual Stanford Cardinal Gus Grumet of University and lost in a three-set battle to Dylan Donovan of Head-Royce as a junior. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3. Smolko entered as the top seed, beating Alameda’s Johnny Sanchez 6-0, 6-1 in the first round, CV’s Matthew Rodriguez 6-0, 6-2 in the quarterfinals, and Bishop O’Dowd’s Marcello Sachelari 6-1, 6-3 in the semifinals. DAHLIA OSMAN Flag Football, Girls’ Lacrosse Dahlia Osman concludes her athletic career at Piedmont High as a three-year starter on the flag Lucas Smolko was named the school’s Outstanding Male Senior Athlete. football team, and two-year varsity member of the girls’ lacrosse team. On the gridiron, Osman represents the school’s hallmark player from flag football’s inaugural years, finishing with 24 total interceptions in three years. She earned first-team All-League honors in 2024 and 2025, and an honorable mention in 2023. She converted from the cornerback role in 2023, to captaining the defense the next two years from the safety spot. In addition to interceptions and pass breakups, she led the team in tackles for the last two years. In lacrosse, Osman grew from a substitute role in 2025 to being a fulltime starter in 2026. The Highlanders went 6-11 this season, while she was a member of PHS’ 2025 team that reached the D2 NCS Championship game as the No. 6 seed before falling 11-10 in sudden-death overtime to No. 4 College Park. After primarily contributing as a defender in 2025, she emerged as an offensive threat as a senior. She logged a hat trick in Piedmont’s 6-5 win over San Rafael on April 1. Dahlia Osman was named Piedmont High’s girls’ Outstanding Senior Athlete. She’s pictured with flag football assistant coach Hayley Adams (left) and head coach Beth Black.

articles.text: While the club season has completed for most indoor girls volleyball players, Piedmont is seeing seven of its players continuing with post-season practices to prepare for the prestigious USA Volleyball Junior Nationals on June 19-22 in Minnesota. These seven Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School players from two Bay Area volleyball clubs– San Rafael’s Absolute and Walnut Creek’s Red Rock– have been invited to compete at the highest level of girls volleyball, playing against other top players across the country. PHS sophomore Allyson Huynh will join her team, Absolute 15 Black, in Indianapolis, where they will compete in the Liberty division at USAV Nationals. Absolute 15 Black competed in the 2026 Northern California Volleyball Association Regional Finals with a 2nd place finish on May 10 out of 136 teams in the age group. The team also competed at the Northeast Qualifier tournament in Philadelphia, PA, winning the tournament on April 5 and qualifying the team to play in the Liberty division at Nationals. This will be Huynh’s second appearance at Nationals. Huynh plays defensive specialist/libero for Absolute and is a setter and right-side hitter (opposite side or “Oppo”) for PHS. PHS freshmen Hazel Schaffer and Carina Vora from Red Rock 15 earned a bid to Nationals after a dramatic finish at NCVA Regional Finals. The team entered the final weekend ranked No. 16 following strong showings in qualifier tournaments in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City, narrowly missing earlier bid opportunities. Needing to climb into the top 15 to secure a bid, they faced immediate pressure from Huynh’s team, perennial powerhouse, Absolute 15 Black. After a hard-fought loss, the path became clear: win three straight matches to earn an invitation, or else the season ends. Behind elite setting, steady leadership and high level defensive play, team co-captain and libero Schaffer and setter Vora helped guide the team through a clutch three-match run. Their performance propelled the team to an 11th place finish on May 10, earning the team a Freedom bid to Nationals. Schaffer is a libero/defensive specialist and outside hitter for PHS, and Vora is a setter for PHS. At the 14s level: Piedmont Middle School 8th grader Campbell Miller will head to Nationals in Indianapolis with an Open bid. Her team Absolute 14 Black dominated the Northern California and Nevada competition, finishing the season No. 1 out of 143 teams in her age group in NCVA. Absolute 14 Black played in three national qualifier tournaments in the highest Open division, just narrowly missing a bid each time. In recognition of their play caliber, the team was awarded an At-Large Open bid by USAV at the close of the regular season. Miller plays middle blocker for Absolute and the PMS 8th grade team. Also from the same volleyball club, PMS 8th grader Sarina Hill will be at Nationals competing in the USA division for the third consecutive year. Her team Absolute 14 Pink earned a No. Piedmont volleyball players Allyson Huynh (top left), Campbell Miller, Sarina Hill, Sofie Bechtel, Liva Olsen; (bottom photo) Carina Vora (left), and Hazel Schaffer will feature at the USA Volleyball Junior Nationals. 6 ranking to close the 2026 season, a rare feat where two teams from the same club finish in gold. Their finish also gave the team the distinction of double-bidding for Nationals when they earned a USA division bid based on their season-close results. Earlier in the season, Absolute 14 Pink competed in the Pacific Northwest Qualifier tournament in Spokane, WA which they won commandingly. Not a single set was dropped on their road to victory at that tournament, and the team received its first bid, in the Liberty division, to Nationals on April 5. Hill is a libero/defensive specialist for Absolute, and she plays several roles, including setter and libero, for the PMS 8th grade team. At the 13s level: Sofie Bechtel, a PMS 8th grader, competes on Absolute 13 Black. The team started the season ranked No. 7 out of 105 teams in their age group from Northern California and Nevada and remained in the NCVA gold bracket throughout the season. The team capped off the season with a 5th place finish at Regional Finals on May 10, securing the team a Liberty bid to Nationals. USAV Nationals for this age group will be played in Minnesota, and this will be Bechtel’s second appearance playing at this elite level. Bechtel is a libero/ defensive specialist for Absolute and an outside hitter for the PMS 8th grade team. PMS 7th grader Liva Olsen will be seeing Bechtel in Minnesota in June. Olsen is a leftie playing oppo for Absolute 13 Pink. The team earned its bid to Nationals at the Pacific Northwest Qualifier tournament in Spokane, WA, where on the final day, Absolute 13 Pink ironically faced its local nemesis, a team from Sacramento, while both teams were 1,000 miles away from home. Absolute 13 Pink battled hard, winning the tie-break 3rd set to finish the tournament in 3rd place and earning a bid to Nationals in the Liberty division. Olsen is an oppo for Absolute and an outside hitter for the PMS 7th grade team.

With no time to dwell on their defeat, the Scots returned home to Witter Field the next day to take on Albany Middle School in the semi-finals of the EBMSL playoffs. The capacity crowd would not be disappointed as the matchup delivered a riveting display of high-quality play and dramatic moments in a fun-filled atmosphere. The Scots came out strong with 8th grade ace, Madi Farboud, keeping the Cobras in check from the circle and Bailey Gregovich once again jumpstarting the offense with an early HR. The Cobras would eventually find their bite, breaking through with some aggressive base runAbby Gregovich hit the game-winner to solidify a 7-6 win in the semifinals. ning and a few timely hits. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team made it to the quarterfinals of the Division 5 North Coast Section postseason as the No. 6 seed before losing to No. 3 Willits 17-7 on the Wolverines home field in Mendocino County on Friday, May 22. To get there, Piedmont defeated No. 11 California School for the Deaf 18-11 at Witter Field on Tuesday, May 19. They conclude their season with a 13-11 record. Their quarterfinals appearance marked the third year in a row for Piedmont to reach the round. This year, they did so with a roster that had no seniors, two juniors, four sophomores, and a whopping eight freshmen. “We have a lot of underclassmen, so this year was a learning year and have fun. A lot of these young ladies don’t have a big background in softball and are learning. Hopefully, we’ll have some good years ahead as we gain experience,” said coach Gene Denard. The Highlanders move toward 2027 with some potential building blocks o m place. Freshman Talia Perl emerged as their Day 1 starting pitcher. Sophomore Edie Elmquist appears at short stop and carried a team-high .542 batting average and 55 runs scored, and 35 stolen bases. Sophomore Hannah Joerger, meanwhile, led the team with 42 hits and 55 RBIs, to go along with a .525 batting average. Freshman Rosemary Dickinson was third on the team with 18 hits, 23 RBIs, and a .295 batting average. 17-7 loss to Willits Piedmont took a 4-1 lead following the top of the second, but Willits tied it in the bottom half and then went up 10-4 in the third inning. PHS scored three runs in the top of the fourth, but conceded four in the bottom half, and another three in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hailey Navarro scored one run. Perl drew a walk. Joerger went 2-for-3. Dickinson went 1-for-3 with a double and one RBI. Elmquist had one run and one walk. Talati scored one run. Teah Suhr went 1-for-2 with two runs scored. Penelope Hopper went 1-for-2 with two RBIs and one walk. Samantha Schey had one run scored. Makenna Small went 1-for-3 with one run scored and one stolen base. Hannah Joerger had three RBIs on two hits against California School for the Deaf, and two hits against Willits. articles.text: Soprano Shannon Crowley The San Francisco Opera will conclude its 2026 Schwabacher Recital Series on June 16 with a performance featuring American bass-baritone Kyle Ketelsen and pianist Carrie-Ann Matheson alongside participants from the 2026 Merola Opera Program. The recital will include performances by soprano Shannon Crowley, soprano Charlotte Kelso, tenor Chester Seungyup Han, tenor Ryan Bryce Johnson, baritone Paul Jang and pianist Deven Shah. The program features works by Maurice Ravel, Henri Duparc, Gioachino Rossini, Giuseppe Verdi, Antonio Schira and Ottorino Respighi, as well as excerpts from Act I of Don Giovanni and Act II of Tosca. Ketelsen, who made his San Francisco Opera debut as Escamillo in Carmen in 2006, is appearing this season in the title role of Don Giovanni at the Metropolitan Opera. He will also return to San Francisco this month to perform Orest in Elektra under Music Director Eun Sun Kim. Matheson, artistic director of the San Francisco Opera Center and Merola Opera Program, has worked internationally as a pianist, conductor and vocal coach. A former assistant conductor and coach at the Metropolitan Opera, she has collaborated with singers including Joyce DiDonato and Jonas Kaufmann. The concert is held Tuesday, June 16, at 7 p.m. at Barbro Osher Recital Hall in San Francisco. The Schwabacher Recital Series presents emerging and esteemed artists from around the globe, primarily alumni or faculty of Merola Opera Program. Visit www.sfopera.com to learn more and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Osaka-born, Berlin-based artist Chiharu Shiota’s first solo museum exhibition in the Bay Area is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Titled Two Home Countries, the exhibition spans the artist’s career across installation, sculpture, video, drawing and stage design. Shiota is best known for immersive environments constructed from densely woven strands of colored yarn, and presenting large-scale installations and other works that explore themes of identity, memory and belonging. At the center of the exhibition is Diary, a monumental installation that fills the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion. Red threads extend across the 88-foot gallery, surrounding visitors as suspended handwritten pages from Japanese soldiers and postwar German civilians hang overhead. “Shiota is interested in what remains after a person is gone,” said Chief Curator Robert Mintz. “The installation makes history feel personal, fragmented, and profoundly present.” Other works include Two Home Countries, in which a red dress unravels into cords connecting two house-like structures, as well as sketches and videos documenting Shiota’s stage design work for KINKAKUJI (The Temple of the Golden Pavilion). “Chiharu Shiota’s work resonates because it makes emotional states visible,” Asian Art Museum Director Soyoung Lee said in a press release. “Her installations speak to the experience of living between places, histories, and identities — an experience that feels increasingly familiar to many people today.” Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/chiharu-shiota-two-home-countries/ to learn more.
articles.title: Chiharu Shiota exhibition on view now at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) is hosting a Spring Sing concert to honor the graduating class of 2026 and the accomplishments of all ensembles from all their choirs in this grand season finale. The event takes place on Saturday, May 30, from 3 - 5 p.m. at the Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church (1801 Lacassie Avenue). The concert includes an annual serenade of Homeward Bound to a curated program of highlights from their 2025-26 season. This includes pieces the touring choirs are taking with them on their tours for the remainder of the year. This annual culmination concert of our season provides inspiration and community for the whole family. The participating PEBCC Choirs are: T1, T2, T3, Ancora, Ecco, Ensemble, and Concert Choir. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir was established in 1982 when, at the request of community leader Susan Rahl, the twenty-two founding members of the “Piedmont Boys Choir” first gathered under the direction of founding Artistic Director Robert Geary. The Choir’s founding principles were to teach the fundamentals and art of music and perform to the highest standard in a creative and supportive environment. The Choirs have always maintained these core principles, while championing new music for youth choirs and increasingly focusing on social justice and global citizenship. Tickets are $30 for adults. Tickets for seniors, students, alumni, or children ages 6 and older are $20. Those interested in volunteering will receive a free ticket. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony concludes its 2026 Chamber Series with a curated program highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 31. The series closes with “I, Too, Sing America,” curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. Smith currently serves as the Director of Music and Organist at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. He previously served as Director of Music and Organist at the Historic Third Baptist Church of San Francisco and was the Founding Director of the Bridge to Arts and Music Program in association with the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton in a press release. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvořák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ SymJames Parrish Smith phony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” The 2025/26 season also marks the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful sixyear tenure. Young first guest-conducted the Berkeley Symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute conductor. articles.text: The Girls’ Choir Canzona One of the international youth choirs participating in this year’s Golden Gate International Music Festival, hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, is the Girls’ Choir Canzona from Poland. Founded in 1981, the ensemble consists of 65 singers divided into two age groups: 7 to 12 and 13 to 19. Canzona is a laureate of numerous prestigious competitions. The choir’s spotlight performance will take place on July 15 at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. For more than forty years, the choir has performed extensively in Poland and abroad, including concerts in Germany, Italy, Spain, Croatia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Israel, Malta, France, Portugal, and Vietnam. The ensemble has been honored to sing for Pope John Paul II several times. Since 2008, the choir has collaborated on organizing the International Choral Festival in Murowana Goślina. The founder and long-time conductor Prof. Elżbieta Wtorkowska currently leads the women’s ensemble and provides artistic and substantive supervision to the girls’ choir and the Canzona Kameralna ensemble, led by Adrianna Wtorkowska-Kubińska and Magdalena Holec. With the Canzona choirs, she has performed in Germany, Switzerland, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Russia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Finland, Austria, Ukraine, England, Spain, Portugal, Bulgaria, and Greece. Its most important achievements include: a Gold Diploma at the 25th National Sea Song Competition in Wejherowo in 2022, a Gold Diploma at the International Choral Competition and Festival Cançó Mediterrània in Spain, a Gold Diploma at the National Patriotic Song Competition Musica Patriae in Poznań, and a Gold Diploma in sacred music at the International Choral Competition Chorus in Croatia in 2023. In 2024, the choir received a Gold Diploma at the National Christmas Carol Competition in Wrocław and First Prize at the European Music Festival for Young People in Belgium. In 2025, the choir won a Gold Diploma, first place in the youth choir category, and a Grand Prix nomination at the Vietnam International Choir Competition, as well as the Grand Prix and Best Conductor Award at the National Choral Competition in Lubostroń. The choir also received two Gold Diplomas at the international Chorus Inside competition in Italy. Held every three years and now in its 13th year, the Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place this year from July 13 to July 18. articles.text: Hayao Miyazaki, writer, director, and animator is not only one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, but his extraordinary talent is venerated worldwide. His deep bench of award-wining animated films, each hand-drawn, using watercolor and acrylic paints, are considered so beautifully detailed (every frame stands alone) and judged to be works of art. Studio Ghibli has long resisted using computer-generated animation. Miyazaki’s thematic storytelling is compelling, often focusing on environmentalism, youthful independence, risk, and the cost of war. As well, his protagonists are often strong, young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his profound impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors, and writers. Within a very short period, streaming has all but revolutionized what was once simply referred to as “going to the movies.” Films that were released in theaters for a limited time (hence often missed) are now available. If your youngster missed, say, Studio Ghibli’s Oscar-winning Spirited Away (2001) and The Boy and the Heron (2024), both are now streaming. All that’s required today is a television (likely wide-screen), and a subscription to, say, Prime, Netflix, Fandango, Apple tv, or Disney+. Don’t forget the popcorn. The name Studio Ghibli was chosen by Miyazaki in 1985. Surprisingly, the noun “Ghibli” references Italy’s Saharan scout plane, the Caproni Ca. 309, melded with the Arabic word for hot desert wind.

It is a compelling fairytale-adventure that will captivate its young audience. The narrative opens with Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), a young girl, 10, sitting in the backseat of the family car. Her arms are crossed, her attitude is petulant; she’s clearly not happy. The family – mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) – have decided to move to the countryside. Chihiro is already missing her friends. As it turns out they take a wrong turn, enter a tunnel, and discover they are in what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. Spotting a restaurant, they go in and her parents begin to eat. Chihiro wanders away and soon runs into a boy her own age, Haku (Jason Marsden), who takes her on a tour of the park. When she returns to the restaurant she discovers that her parents have been transformed into pigs. She learns that this shocking change was brought about by a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette) who runs a bathhouse for tired spirits. Haku warns Chihiro to avoid the witch, but she is told she must serve the malevolent hag in order to return her parents to their original forms. articles.text: Nestled high in the rugged hills of California’s Central Coast, Calera Wine Company has long been regarded as one of America’s most influential Pinot Noir producers. Located near the small town of Hollister in the remote Gavilan Mountains, Calera helped prove that world-class Pinot Noir could be made outside of Burgundy long before California’s Central Coast became fashionable. The winery was founded in 1975 by visionary winemaker Josh Jensen, whose fascination with Burgundy led him on an unusual journey. After studying winemaking and working harvests in France, Jensen searched California for limestone-rich soils similar to those of Burgundy’s Côte d’Or. He eventually found them in the isolated limestone deposits of San Benito County and established Calera on a mountaintop site that many at the time considered too remote and inhospitable for fine wine. That sense of isolation became one of Calera’s defining strengths. Cool nights, high elevations, and rocky limestone soils allowed the winery to produce wines with unusual finesse and structure. At a time when many California wines emphasized ripeness and power, Calera pursued elegance, balance, and age-worthiness. Jensen often spoke about allowing the vineyard to speak for itself rather than overpowering the wine through excessive oak or manipulation. Over the decades, Calera earned a near-cult reputation for elegant, age-worthy Pinot Noir wines that emphasized restraint, minerality, and site expression. articles.text: Scooter the Great Dane runs a FastCat 100-yard dash in 8.3 seconds! Despite the convenience of a dog small enough to fit in your purse, many owners lose their hearts to giant breeds like mastiffs and great danes. These gentle giants are some of the most loving dogs out there. Although they often have shorter lifespans than smaller breeds, the years spent with these extra-large loves are full of affection and laughter. Special size comes with special needs, and many giant breeds simply aren’t built for high-impact work, preferring to cuddle on the couch. However, they still need exercise! The following activities are tailored to giant breed needs. If you’re looking for relaxing activities you can do almost anywhere, consider hiking or walking on natural terrain such as dirt trails or grass. Brisk walks in these environments provide exercise while sparing the dog’s joints from repeated impact on concrete. Swimming is another excellent option: a fun, low-impact, full-body workout. Be sure to bring a doggy life jacket. Despite their cumbersome size, giant breed dogs can excel at certain dog sports. One of these sports is Fast CAT, a timed 100- yard dash where a mechanical lure stimulates the dog’s natural prey drive. Dogs earn titles and awards for participation. Giant breeds may also enjoy dock diving, where dogs leap from a dock in pursuit of a toy. Because these sports are performed in short bursts, they can be excellent choices for dogs with lower stamina or low-impact exercise needs. For mental enrichment, consider puzzle toys that are large, durable, and food-dispensing to keep your dog motivated. Cue your dog to “find it!” and time how long it takes them to locate hidden items at varying levels of difficulty, similar to the AKC Virtual Scent Work program. And let’s not forget trick training. While giant breeds may not be suited for acrobatic tricks, they can shine with oversized props for added humor, such as giant beach balls or even pulling smaller dogs in a wagon. When engaging in these activities, remember a few important safety tips. Avoid intense exercise on concrete to protect joints. Giant breeds can also overheat quickly, so opt for early morning or evening exercise during warm weather. Regular veterinary checkups are important before beginning intense sports, and activity should always be avoided immediately after meals to prevent bloat. Although giant breed dogs may seem like perfect couch potatoes, they can also be wonderful companions in outdoor activities and sports. Because their time with us is often shorter, it’s worth making the effort to create lasting memories with your gentle giant. Whether you’re hiking a trail, splashing in the water, or teaching a silly new trick, the most important thing is spending time together and including your pup in the fun. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: Photos by Ethan Shrago and Jim Mehlinger The Scouts enjoyed a ride through the countryside at the Western Railroad Museum on a restored 1930s electric train. The train interior displays advertisements from bygone eras. Left — front to back: Steve Belcher, Ethan Shrago, Rudy Campanillo, Stephen Campanillo, Quartermaster Ryan Moon, Andrew Lavin, Quartermaster Leo Shrago, and Gabe Tucker. Right — front to back: Jim Mehlinger, Assistant Scoutmaster Jen Ferguson, David Ferguson, Julie Veit, Forrest Poole, Christian Tran, Senior Patrol Leader Ted Eisemon, Patrol Leader Jojo Shim, and Bennie Belcher. Ted Eisemon Members of Piedmont Troop 11 rode historic trains to earn the Railroad Merit Badge. The May 3 adventure was organized and led by Quartermaster Leo Shrago and Assistant Scoutmaster Jen Ferguson. Merit Badges are awarded to Scouts who have learned skills, explored hobbies, or investigated possible careers in over a hundred areas. Merit badge activities promote self-confidence, learning, life skills, and personal growth. Scouts earn the Railroad Merit Badge by studying the history, technology, safety, and career opportunities in the railroad industry. They must learn about freight and passenger operations, signals, and modern digital communications and command controls. Scouts must also complete a hands-on activity such as visiting a train museum or “rail fanning,” which includes riding trains. The Scouts enjoyed a ride through the countryside at the Western Railroad Museum in Suisun City on a restored 1930s electric train. The train interior displayed vintage advertisements from bygone eras. Outside was rolling countryside with cattle ranches, rabbits scurrying from the tracks, elk grazing in the distance, and an extensive modern windmill array. They enjoyed a guided tour of the train shed filled with a variety of trains from old steam locomotives to early BART cars. After a question and answer meeting with a train engineer, the Scouts drove to the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park in Contra Costa County. The railroad builds, restores, and operates narrow-gauge steam trains for passengers. Quartermaster Leo Shrago, who volunteers at the Railway, arranged a guided tour of the train sheds and machine shop. According to his father, Ethan Shrago, Leo has been a train fanatic ever since he was an infant, when he used to fall asleep to the sounds of trains chugging along the track. He quickly moved from Brio wood trains to real model trains. Leo has been a regular visitor to the Redwood Valley Railway since he was 4, always begging to volunteer at the earliest opportunity. Since last summer, he has been working weekly at the track as a brakeman and as a worker in and around the railroad. When Leo heard that this merit badge was available, he jumped at the opportunity to help schedule a day to tackle all the requirements and was excited to share his knowledge and passion about trains with his peers. Troop 11 Scouts ended the day with a ride on the steam train through the forest. If you are interested in information about Scouting in Piedmont or joining Scouts, please visit piedmontscouting.org or email contact@piedmontbsa.org Troop 11 Quartermaster Leo Shrago reviews the written requirements of the Railroad Merit Badge during a lunch break at the Western Railroad Museum. Piedmont Scouts learn about the machine shop and train repair at the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park.

By Jim Mehlinger and Ted Eisemon Members of Piedmont Troop 11 rode historic trains to earn the Railroad Merit Badge. The May 3 adventure was organized and led by Quartermaster Leo Shrago and Assistant Scoutmaster Jen Ferguson. Merit Badges are awarded to Scouts who have learned skills, explored hobbies, or investigated possible careers in over a hundred areas. Merit badge activities promote self-confidence, learning, life skills, and personal growth. Scouts earn the Railroad Merit Badge by studying the history, technology, safety, and career opportunities in the railroad industry. They must learn about freight and passenger operations, signals, and modern digital communications and command controls. Scouts must also complete a hands-on activity such as visiting a train museum or “rail fanning,” which includes riding trains. The Scouts enjoyed a ride through the countryside at the Western Railroad Museum in Suisun City on a restored 1930s electric train. The train interior displayed vintage advertisements from bygone eras. Outside was rolling countryside with cattle ranches, rabbits scurrying from the tracks, elk grazing in the distance, and an extensive modern windmill array. They enjoyed a guided tour of the train shed filled with a variety of trains from old steam locomotives to early BART cars. After a question and answer meeting with a train engineer, the Scouts drove to the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park in Contra Costa County. The railroad builds, restores, and operates narrow-gauge steam trains for passengers. Quartermaster Leo Shrago, who volunteers at the Railway, arranged a guided tour of the train sheds and machine shop. According to his father, Ethan Shrago, Leo has been a train fanatic ever since he was an infant, when he used to fall asleep to the sounds of trains chugging along the track. He quickly moved from Brio wood trains to real model trains. Leo has been a regular visitor to the Redwood Valley Railway since he was 4, always begging to volunteer at the earliest opportunity. Since last summer, he has been working weekly at the track as a brakeman and as a worker in and around the railroad. When Leo heard that this merit badge was available, he jumped at the opportunity to help schedule a day to tackle all the requirements and was excited to share his knowledge and passion about trains with his peers. Troop 11 Scouts ended the day with a ride on the steam train through the forest. If you are interested in information about Scouting in Piedmont or joining Scouts, please visit piedmontscouting.org or email contact@piedmontbsa.org Troop 11 Quartermaster Leo Shrago reviews the written requirements of the Railroad Merit Badge during a lunch break at the Western Railroad Museum. Piedmont Scouts learn about the machine shop and train repair at the Redwood Valley Railroad in Tilden Regional Park. This tax is expiring and must be renewed by voters to preserve the academic programs our students depend on. To maintain the high quality of Piedmont schools, continue funding programs in math, science, technology, engineering, English, music and arts, attract and retain qualified teachers, update instructional materials and technology, and maintain manageable class sizes, shall Piedmont Unified School District’s measure be adopted, renewing the expiring school parcel tax at the current rate ($3,051 per parcel) until ended by voters, with independent citizen oversight, annual inflation adjustments, and all funds (approximately $12 million annually) benefiting local students?
